quizTitle: DevNet Associate - Canvas - Mod01_Act02 Options & Arguments

questions.text: Match each ls option to what it does. The lab only used -l and -r — the rest are standard ls options worth knowing too.
allChoices: Shows every entry, including hidden dotfiles
Long format: shows permissions, owner, size and date
With -l, prints sizes in human-readable units (K, M, G)
Lists the contents of subdirectories too, recursively
Sorts by modification time, newest first
Sorts by file size, largest first

pairs.match: Shows every entry, including hidden dotfiles
Long format: shows permissions, owner, size and date
With -l, prints sizes in human-readable units (K, M, G)
Lists the contents of subdirectories too, recursively
Sorts by modification time, newest first
Sorts by file size, largest first

questions.explanation: Beyond the lab: these are the other ls flags you'll reach for constantly, e.g. ls -lah to see everything, human-sized, in one long listing.

questions.text: Match each cd target to where it takes you.
allChoices: Your home directory
Your home directory (shorthand)
The directory you were in before this one
The root of the entire file system
Exactly one directory level up

pairs.match: Your home directory
Your home directory (shorthand)
The directory you were in before this one
The root of the entire file system
Exactly one directory level up

questions.explanation: The lab only showed /, .. and named subfolders (Part 2). Typing cd alone or cd ~ always jumps home, and cd - is a quick toggle back to your last location.

questions.text: Match each chmod mode to the permission change it makes.
allChoices: Adds execute permission for owner, group and others
Removes execute permission for owner, group and others
Adds write permission for the owner only
Owner gets read/write/execute; group and others get read/execute
Owner gets read/write; group and others get read-only

pairs.match: Adds execute permission for owner, group and others
Removes execute permission for owner, group and others
Adds write permission for the owner only
Owner gets read/write/execute; group and others get read/execute
Owner gets read/write; group and others get read-only

questions.explanation: The lab only used +x (Part 3, Step 2f). chmod also accepts symbolic changes scoped to one category (u/g/o) or a numeric/octal mode like 755, which sets all three categories in one shot.

questions.text: Match each chown argument to what it does.
allChoices: Changes only the owning user
Changes both the owning user and group in one call
Changes only the group, leaving the owner untouched
Applies the ownership change recursively through a directory

pairs.match: Changes only the owning user
Changes both the owning user and group in one call
Changes only the group, leaving the owner untouched
Applies the ownership change recursively through a directory

questions.explanation: The lab only ran sudo chown root myfile.sh (Part 3, Step 2h) — a bare username, which only changes the owner. The user:group and -R forms extend that to the group and to whole directory trees.

questions.text: Match each file-operation flag to what it does.
allChoices: Asks for confirmation before an existing file would be overwritten
Copies a directory and everything inside it
Prints each file's name as it's copied (verbose)
Deletes a directory and everything inside it, recursively
Deletes without prompting, and ignores files that don't exist
Asks for confirmation before deleting each file

pairs.match: Asks for confirmation before an existing file would be overwritten
Copies a directory and everything inside it
Prints each file's name as it's copied (verbose)
Deletes a directory and everything inside it, recursively
Deletes without prompting, and ignores files that don't exist
Asks for confirmation before deleting each file

questions.explanation: The lab's mv/cp/rm calls in Part 3 all ran bare. -r matters most: plain cp or rm refuses to touch a directory without it.

questions.text: Match each echo/cat flag to what it does.
allChoices: Suppresses the trailing newline after the printed text
Interprets backslash escapes like \n and \t in the text
Numbers every line of the output
Displays non-printing characters, like line endings, explicitly

pairs.match: Suppresses the trailing newline after the printed text
Interprets backslash escapes like \n and \t in the text
Numbers every line of the output
Displays non-printing characters, like line endings, explicitly

questions.explanation: The lab's echo and cat calls in Part 3, Step 6 never used flags — these are the ones worth knowing for formatting output or debugging invisible whitespace.

questions.text: Match each redirection/piping operator to what it does.
allChoices: Overwrites the target file with the command's output
Appends the command's output to the end of the target file
Feeds one command's output into a second command as input

pairs.match: Overwrites the target file with the command's output
Appends the command's output to the end of the target file
Feeds one command's output into a second command as input

questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 6 (>, >>) and Part 5, Step 3c (ps -e | more).

questions.text: Match each vi mode key or ex-mode command from the lab to what it does.
allChoices: Enters Edit mode, inserting before the cursor
Enters Edit mode, inserting after the cursor
Returns to Command mode
Writes (saves) the buffer, optionally under a new filename
Quits the editor

questions.text: Match each additional vi Command-mode move to what it does. These go beyond what the lab covered.
allChoices: Deletes (cuts) the entire current line
Yanks (copies) the entire current line
Deletes just the single character under the cursor
Undoes the last change
Writes and quits in one step
Searches forward for the next match of a pattern

pairs.match: Deletes (cuts) the entire current line
Yanks (copies) the entire current line
Deletes just the single character under the cursor
Undoes the last change
Writes and quits in one step

questions.explanation: The lab's Step 7 describes single letters d/y/p loosely; in real vi the line-wise cut and copy are doubled — dd and yy — and there's a lot more to Command mode than the lab shows.

questions.text: Match each grep flag to what it does. The lab never used a flag on grep — every example relied on the bare command plus a pattern.
allChoices: Matches case-insensitively
Inverts the match — shows lines that do NOT match
Prints only a count of matching lines, not the lines themselves
Prefixes each match with its line number
Matches only whole words, not substrings
Searches recursively through every file in a directory

pairs.match: Matches case-insensitively
Inverts the match — shows lines that do NOT match
Prints only a count of matching lines, not the lines themselves
Prefixes each match with its line number
Matches only whole words, not substrings
Searches recursively through every file in a directory

questions.explanation: Part 4 showed grep is case-sensitive by default (Step a) — -i is how you turn that off. The rest round out the flags you'd reach for day to day.

questions.text: Match each regular-expression symbol usable as a grep pattern argument to what it matches.
allChoices: The start of a line
The end of a line
Exactly one of any character
Any single character from the set/range inside
Zero or more of the character right before it

questions.text: Match each way of invoking sudo to what it does. The lab always used the plain form.
allChoices: Opens an interactive root login shell
Runs the command as a specific user, not necessarily root
Lists which commands you're allowed to run with sudo
Runs just that one command with root privileges, then returns to your normal shell

pairs.match: Opens an interactive root login shell
Runs the command as a specific user, not necessarily root
Lists which commands you're allowed to run with sudo
Runs just that one command with root privileges, then returns to your normal shell

questions.explanation: Every sudo call in the lab (Parts 2-5) used this last, plain form — one privileged command at a time, with no new shell created.

questions.text: Match each shutdown argument to what it does.
allChoices: Halts the system immediately
Schedules a shutdown one minute out, broadcasting a message first
Cancels a shutdown that was already scheduled
Reboots the system instead of halting it
Halts (powers down) the system
Powers off the system

pairs.match: Halts the system immediately
Schedules a shutdown one minute out, broadcasting a message first
Cancels a shutdown that was already scheduled
Reboots the system instead of halting it
Halts (powers down) the system
Powers off the system

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 1a-c covers now, the timed form and -c. -r/-h/-P choose what happens once the timer hits zero — reboot vs. halt vs. full power-off.

questions.text: Match each date flag to what it does. The lab ran date completely bare.
allChoices: Prints the date/time using a custom format string
Displays the time in UTC instead of local time
Displays a specified date/time instead of right now
Sets the system clock to a specified date/time (needs root)

pairs.match: Prints the date/time using a custom format string
Displays the time in UTC instead of local time
Displays a specified date/time instead of right now
Sets the system clock to a specified date/time (needs root)

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 2b just called date with no arguments to check the system clock. These flags cover formatting, timezone, hypothetical dates and actually changing the clock.

questions.text: Match each way of running ps to what it shows.
allChoices: Only this terminal's own processes
Every process on the whole system
Every process, with full extended detail such as UID and PPID
Every process for every user, BSD-style, with extra columns like %CPU

pairs.match: Only this terminal's own processes
Every process on the whole system
Every process, with full extended detail such as UID and PPID
Every process for every user, BSD-style, with extra columns like %CPU

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 3a, b and d cover the first three. ps aux is the other listing format you'll see everywhere outside this lab.

questions.text: Match each passwd flag to what it does. The lab only showed -S.
allChoices: Reports the password's status instead of changing it
Locks the account, disabling its password
Unlocks a previously locked account
Forces the password to expire immediately, prompting a change at next login

pairs.match: Reports the password's status instead of changing it
Locks the account, disabling its password
Unlocks a previously locked account
Forces the password to expire immediately, prompting a change at next login

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 5b used -S to check status only. Locking, unlocking and forcing expiry are the other administrative actions passwd can take on an account.

questions.text: Match each ip subcommand to what it shows or does. The lab only used address.
allChoices: Displays the interface and IP address configuration
Shows each interface's link/hardware status
Shows the system's routing table
Assigns a new IP address to an interface

pairs.match: Displays the interface and IP address configuration
Shows each interface's link/hardware status
Shows the system's routing table
Assigns a new IP address to an interface

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 2a used ip address to read the dummy0 interface's five IPs. ip has several other subcommands for reading and changing network state.

questions.text: Match each ping flag to what it does. The lab only used -c.
allChoices: Limits the ping to a fixed number of packets
Sets the interval, in seconds, between packets
Sets how long to wait for a reply before giving up
Sets the size, in bytes, of each packet

pairs.match: Limits the ping to a fixed number of packets
Sets the interval, in seconds, between packets
Sets how long to wait for a reply before giving up
Sets the size, in bytes, of each packet

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 2b used -c 4 to cap the packet count. The others tune the timing and packet size that -c doesn't touch.

questions.text: Match each apt-get subcommand to what it does.
allChoices: Refreshes the local list of packages available from the repositories
Downloads and installs a specific named package
Updates every installed package and dependency on the system
Completely removes a package and its configuration files
Uninstalls a package but keeps its configuration files
Removes packages that were pulled in as dependencies and are no longer needed

pairs.match: Refreshes the local list of packages available from the repositories
Downloads and installs a specific named package
Updates every installed package and dependency on the system
Completely removes a package and its configuration files
Uninstalls a package but keeps its configuration files
Removes packages that were pulled in as dependencies and are no longer needed

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 4a, c, e, f cover update/install/upgrade/purge. remove is purge's gentler sibling, and autoremove is the cleanup step the lab never runs.

questions.text: Match each apt-cache subcommand to what it does. The lab only used search.
allChoices: Looks up a package by keyword in the local cache
Shows a specific package's full details (description, size, dependencies)
Shows a package's installed vs. candidate version and its priority

pairs.match: Looks up a package by keyword in the local cache
Shows a specific package's full details (description, size, dependencies)
Shows a package's installed vs. candidate version and its priority

questions.explanation: Part 5, Step 4b used search to find the exact package name. Once you have that name, show and policy tell you more about it before you install anything.
